question: Does the thing we built solve the problem it was built for?

hevner2004.cite: Hevner et al. (2004). Design science in information systems research. MIS Quarterly 28(1): 75–105.
hevner2004.checked: every quote read word for word in the vault's text copy of the JSTOR PDF (library No. 289) on 20 Nov 2026; page numbers are the journal's, printed on the copy; words broken across lines in the scan are joined; author–year citations inside quotes are left out

steps.title: Pick a real problem
steps.text: Start from a problem people actually have and that has no good solution yet.

quotes.text: The objective of research in information systems is to acquire knowledge and understanding that enable the development and implementation of technology-based solutions to heretofore unsolved and important business problems.

steps.title: Build an artifact
steps.text: Design something that addresses it: a device, a piece of software, a method or a model.

quotes.text: design-science research requires the creation of an innovative, purposeful artifact (Guideline 1) for a specified problem domain (Guideline 2).

steps.title: Evaluate in context
steps.text: Test it with its users where it will be used, with methods suited to the claim: observation, experiments, analysis or tests.

quotes.text: The utility, quality, and efficacy of a design artifact must be rigorously demonstrated via well executed evaluation methods.

steps.title: Build again
steps.text: Use what the evaluation showed to improve the design, and repeat until it works well enough.

quotes.text: This build-and-evaluate loop is typically iterated a number of times before the final design artifact is generated

steps.title: Report to both
steps.text: Write it up for those who will build on it or implement it, and for those who will decide whether to adopt it.

quotes.text: the results of the design-science research must be communicated effectively (Guideline 7) both to a technical audience (researchers who will extend them and practitioners who will implement them) and to a managerial audience

limits: The card's examples (IEC 62366 usability engineering, research software built with its users) are not worked through here; IEC 62366 has not been read.
Hevner et al. (2004) write for information systems; the page applies their guidelines to artifacts in general, as the card does.
